lessons.title: The Three Big Questions Every Company Faces

blocks.robotComment: Every finance decision a company ever makes is really just one of three questions. Learn these and the rest of this track clicks into place. 🏢
blocks.body: Corporate finance is the study of how companies make money decisions, and nearly every one of those decisions boils down to three questions: what should we invest in, how should we pay for it, and what should we do with any money left over? These are usually called the investing decision, the financing decision, and the payout decision.

The investing decision covers things like building a new factory, launching a product, or acquiring another company — anything the company spends money on hoping it pays off later. The financing decision covers how that spending gets funded: borrowing money, selling shares, or using cash the company already has. The payout decision covers what happens to profit: reinvest it, pay it out as a dividend, or buy back shares.

highlights.text: reinvest it, pay it out as a dividend, or buy back shares

blocks.sentence: The decision about how to fund a company's spending — borrowing, selling shares, or using existing cash — is called the ___ decision.
blocks.explanation: The financing decision is specifically about how money is raised to fund whatever the investing decision chose to spend on.

blocks.robotComment: This framework is the spine of this whole track — everything from here on is really just zooming into one of these three. 🦴
blocks.body: This three-question framework is the spine of this entire track. Reading financial statements, valuing a company, understanding mergers, and building a financial model are all really just different tools for answering one of these three questions more precisely, for a real company in a real situation.

highlights.text: the spine of this entire track

blocks.question: Which of the following are the three core questions of corporate finance?
options: What to invest in, how to finance it, and what to do with leftover profit
How to hire employees, where to open an office, and what to name the company
What color the logo should be, and two unrelated questions
Only one question: how to make the stock price go up
blocks.explanation: The investing, financing, and payout decisions are the classic three-question framework at the core of corporate finance.

blocks.statement: The payout decision covers what a company does with leftover profit, such as reinvesting it, paying dividends, or buying back shares.
blocks.explanation: That's exactly what the payout decision covers — what happens to profit once it exists.

blocks.robotComment: Pop culture makes this job look like non-stop shouting on a trading floor. The reality is very different, and honestly more interesting. 💼
blocks.body: Investment bankers primarily advise companies on two things: raising money (helping a company sell stock or bonds to investors) and mergers & acquisitions (helping a company buy, sell, or combine with another company). This is different from a trader, who buys and sells securities, and different from a financial advisor, who works with individual people's personal investments.

A huge amount of the actual day-to-day work is analytical: building financial models, valuing companies, preparing presentation materials, and researching industries — much of it covered later in this track. The glamorous moments (a company going public, a headline-making acquisition) are the visible tip of a much larger amount of careful, detailed work behind the scenes.

highlights.text: a much larger amount of careful, detailed work

blocks.sentence: Investment bankers primarily advise companies on raising money and ___ — buying, selling, or combining with other companies.
blocks.explanation: M&A advisory, alongside helping companies raise capital, is the core of what investment bankers actually do.

blocks.robotComment: Level 8 goes much deeper into the career itself, including the honest trade-offs — this is just the first look. 🔎
blocks.body: This track doesn't assume you want to become an investment banker specifically — the skills here (reading financial statements, valuing companies, understanding how deals work) are genuinely useful for anyone trying to understand business and investing at a deeper level, whatever career path you're actually on. Level 8 does look at the career path itself in more depth, honestly, including its real trade-offs.

blocks.question: How does an investment banker's role differ from a trader's?
options: A banker primarily advises companies on raising money and deals, while a trader buys and sells securities
They are exactly the same job with different titles
A trader only works with individual people's retirement accounts
A banker never works with numbers or financial models
blocks.explanation: Investment banking is an advisory role focused on corporate transactions, distinct from trading, which is about buying and selling securities.

blocks.statement: Most of an investment banker's actual day-to-day work is dramatic, headline-making deal moments.
blocks.explanation: The visible headline moments are a small fraction of the work — most of the actual job is detailed analytical work like modeling and valuation.

lessons.title: Reading a Company From the Outside

blocks.robotComment: This track hands you the same lens professionals actually use to size up a company. 🔬
blocks.body: Every publicly traded company is required to publish detailed financial information, which means the same tools professionals use to evaluate a business are available to anyone willing to learn how to read them. This track teaches exactly that: how to look at a company from the outside — through its public numbers — and form a genuine, informed view.

This connects directly to two other tracks in this app: Investing Fundamentals covers what stocks and funds are, and Stock Market & Trading covers reading a quote and the market itself. This track goes a level deeper — how to actually evaluate the business behind the ticker symbol, not just its price.

highlights.text: the business behind the ticker symbol

blocks.sentence: Publicly traded companies are required to publish detailed ___ information, which anyone can learn to read.
blocks.explanation: Public disclosure requirements are exactly what make it possible for anyone to learn to evaluate a company's business, not just its stock price.

blocks.robotComment: By the end of this track, a company's numbers will tell you a real story, not just a wall of digits. 📖
blocks.body: By the end of this track, the goal is that a company's financial statements stop looking like an intimidating wall of numbers and start reading like a story: how it makes money, how healthy it actually is, what it's worth, and how it compares to others in its industry. That skill is valuable whether or not you ever work in finance professionally.

options: Public companies are required to publish detailed financial information that anyone can access and learn to read
Only licensed professionals are legally allowed to see company financials
Company financials are guessed rather than reported
This track requires an insider connection at the company
blocks.explanation: Public disclosure requirements make company financials genuinely available to anyone willing to learn how to read them.

blocks.statement: This track focuses only on stock prices, not on the underlying business behind a company.
blocks.explanation: This track goes a level deeper than price — into the actual business behind the ticker symbol, complementing the Investing Fundamentals and Stock Market & Trading tracks.

blocks.robotComment: Think of it as the company's report card for a stretch of time, not a photo of one single day. 🎬
blocks.body: The income statement — sometimes called the profit & loss statement, or P&L — shows how much money a company made and spent over a period of time, like a quarter or a full year. Unlike a balance sheet, which is a single snapshot, the income statement is more like a video: it captures a stretch of activity from the first day of the period to the last.

The structure follows a simple logic: start with revenue (money earned from selling products or services), subtract the direct cost of producing what was sold to get gross profit, subtract operating expenses like salaries, rent, and marketing to get operating income, and subtract interest and taxes to arrive at net income — the number often called "the bottom line."

code.code:
Revenue                     $500M
Cost of Goods Sold           -$200M
--------------------------------------
Gross Profit                  $300M

Operating Expenses            -$180M
--------------------------------------
Operating Income (EBIT)        $120M

Interest & Taxes                -$45M
--------------------------------------
Net Income                      $75M
code.caption: Brightleaf Coffee Co.'s income statement for the year: revenue minus costs and expenses, step by step, down to net income of $75 million.

blocks.sentence: On an income statement, revenue minus the cost of goods sold equals ___.
blocks.explanation: Gross profit is the first major subtotal — revenue minus the direct cost of producing what was sold.

blocks.robotComment: You'll see Brightleaf again in the balance sheet and cash flow lessons — same company, three different views of it. 👀
blocks.body: This lesson follows one illustrative example company throughout this level: Brightleaf Coffee Co., a fictional coffee chain. Brightleaf earned $500 million in revenue this year, and after all its costs, expenses, interest, and taxes, its net income — its actual profit — was $75 million. That $75 million is what's available to reinvest in the business, pay down debt, or return to shareholders.

blocks.question: Brightleaf Coffee Co. has revenue of $500 million and cost of goods sold of $200 million. What is its gross profit?
blocks.explanation: Gross profit is revenue minus cost of goods sold: $500M - $200M = $300M.

blocks.robotComment: Keep this distinction in your back pocket — it's the very next lesson. 🔑
blocks.statement: The income statement shows a company's financial position at a single point in time, like a snapshot.
blocks.explanation: That description fits the balance sheet. The income statement covers a period of time, like a quarter or a year — more like a video than a snapshot.

blocks.robotComment: This equation has to balance, literally — that's where the name comes from. ⚖️
blocks.body: The balance sheet shows what a company owns, owes, and is worth at a single point in time — a snapshot, not a video. It's built on one equation that must always hold true: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. What the company owns must equal what it owes to creditors plus what belongs to its owners.

Assets are everything the company owns that has value: cash, money owed to it by customers (accounts receivable), inventory, and equipment. Liabilities are everything it owes to others: unpaid bills (accounts payable), and debt. Equity is what's left over for the owners once liabilities are subtracted from assets — it's not a pile of cash sitting somewhere, but a calculated ownership stake.

code.code:
Assets
Cash                          $50M
Accounts Receivable          $40M
Inventory                     $60M
Property & Equipment         $350M
----------------------------------
Total Assets                  $500M

Liabilities
Accounts Payable              $30M
Short-Term Debt                $20M
Long-Term Debt                $200M
----------------------------------
Total Liabilities             $250M

Equity                         $250M
(Total Assets - Total Liabilities)
code.caption: Brightleaf Coffee Co.'s balance sheet: $500M in total assets exactly equals $250M in liabilities plus $250M in equity.

blocks.sentence: The balance sheet always follows the equation: Assets = Liabilities + ___.
blocks.explanation: Equity is the owners' stake — what's left over after subtracting everything the company owes from everything it owns.

blocks.robotComment: Hold onto that thread — "how the three statements connect" picks it back up. 🧵
blocks.body: Notice the difference from the income statement: the balance sheet doesn't ask "how much did the company earn this year?" — it asks "what does the company own and owe right now, today?" Brightleaf's $75 million in net income from the income statement doesn't appear directly on the balance sheet as its own line item; instead, it flows into equity, which the next path in this level explains.

highlights.text: what does the company own and owe right now, today?

blocks.question: Brightleaf has total assets of $500 million and total liabilities of $250 million. What is its equity?
blocks.explanation: Equity = Assets - Liabilities = $500M - $250M = $250M.

blocks.statement: The balance sheet shows a company's financial activity over an entire year, similar to the income statement.
blocks.explanation: The balance sheet is a snapshot at a single point in time, not a record of activity over a period — that's the income statement's job.

lessons.title: The Cash Flow Statement, Simply Explained

blocks.robotComment: Three sections, one question each: cash from the business, cash from investments, cash from financing. 💵
blocks.body: The cash flow statement tracks actual cash moving in and out of a company over a period of time — not accounting profit, but real money hitting or leaving the bank account. It's organized into three sections: cash from operating activities (the core business), investing activities (buying or selling long-term assets), and financing activities (borrowing, repaying debt, or paying dividends).

Brightleaf's operating activities start with net income and adjust for non-cash items like depreciation, plus changes in things like receivables and payables. Investing activities capture the $60 million it spent on new equipment. Financing activities capture debt repayment and dividends paid to shareholders. Adding all three sections together gives the total change in cash for the period.

code.code:
Cash from Operating Activities        $95M
Cash from Investing Activities        -$60M
Cash from Financing Activities        -$25M
----------------------------------------------
Net Change in Cash                     $10M

Beginning Cash Balance                 $40M
Ending Cash Balance                    $50M
code.caption: Brightleaf's three sections combine to a $10 million increase in cash, taking its cash balance from $40M to $50M — matching the $50M cash figure on its balance sheet.

blocks.sentence: The cash flow statement is organized into operating, investing, and ___ activities.
blocks.explanation: The three sections are operating, investing, and financing activities.

blocks.robotComment: That single sentence is the whole reason this statement exists. 🎯
blocks.body: Why does this statement exist at all, if the income statement already shows profit? Because profit and cash are not the same thing, for reasons the next lesson explores in detail. A company can report a healthy net income and still run low on actual cash — or the reverse. The cash flow statement is often considered the hardest of the three statements to fake, since cash either moved or it didn't.

highlights.text: profit and cash are not the same thing

blocks.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three sections of the cash flow statement?
blocks.explanation: The three sections are operating, investing, and financing activities — marketing isn't one of the statement's sections, though marketing spending does show up inside operating activities.

blocks.statement: The cash flow statement tracks the same thing as the income statement — accounting profit.
blocks.explanation: The cash flow statement tracks actual cash moving in and out, which can differ meaningfully from the accounting profit reported on the income statement.

blocks.robotComment: Once you can see these threads, the three statements stop feeling like three separate documents. 🧵
blocks.body: Each financial statement covers different ground, but they're not independent — they're three views of the same underlying company, and they connect through specific numbers. The clearest connection starts with net income, the bottom line of the income statement.

Net income flows into the cash flow statement as the very first line of cash from operating activities — Brightleaf's $75 million in net income is the starting point before the adjustments discussed in the previous lesson. Net income also flows into the balance sheet: after dividends are paid out, whatever profit remains gets added to retained earnings, a component of equity.

highlights.text: cash flow statement as the very first line

code.code:
Beginning Equity                    $190M
+ Net Income                          $75M
- Dividends Paid                     -$15M
----------------------------------------
Ending Equity                        $250M
code.caption: Net income flows into equity: after $15M in dividends, the remaining $60M of profit increases Brightleaf's equity from $190M to $250M — matching the balance sheet.

blocks.sentence: Net income first appears on the income statement, then becomes the starting line of the cash flow statement's ___ activities section.
blocks.explanation: Net income is the first line item in the cash from operating activities section, which then gets adjusted for non-cash items and working capital changes.

blocks.body: This is why the three statements are often described as connected, not separate: pull one thread — net income — and it shows up on all three statements in a different form. Analysts sometimes build all three statements together in a single spreadsheet model specifically because a change to one, like a jump in revenue, ripples through the other two automatically.

blocks.question: Which figure, once it appears on the income statement, also flows into both the cash flow statement and the balance sheet?
blocks.explanation: Net income is the connecting thread: it starts the cash flow statement's operating section and, after dividends, adds to equity on the balance sheet.

blocks.statement: The three financial statements are essentially independent documents that don't relate to one another.
blocks.explanation: They're three connected views of the same company — net income alone links the income statement to both the cash flow statement and the balance sheet.

lessons.title: Why Profit Isn't the Same as Cash

blocks.robotComment: A company can look great on the income statement and still struggle to pay its bills. That gap is exactly what this lesson is about. 💡
blocks.body: Accounting profit is recognized when a sale is made, not necessarily when cash actually arrives. This gap between "earned on paper" and "collected in the bank" is one of the most important — and most misunderstood — ideas in reading financial statements.

highlights.text: recognized when a sale is made, not necessarily when cash actually arrives

blocks.body: Suppose in its final month of the year, Brightleaf lands a large catering contract with a corporate client: $8 million in revenue, with the client paying on 60-day terms. Accounting rules say Brightleaf recognizes the revenue — and the profit — immediately, the moment it delivers the service. If the costs tied to that contract were $3 million, this single deal adds $5 million to net income for the month. But not one dollar of that $8 million has actually reached Brightleaf's bank account yet.

code.code:
Catering Contract Revenue          $8.0M
Costs Tied to the Contract         -$3.0M
------------------------------------------
Added to Net Income (on paper)      $5.0M

Cash Actually Collected So Far      $0.0M
(Client pays in 60 days)
code.caption: The $5M profit is real under accounting rules, but the cash is still 60 days away — it currently sits as accounts receivable, not cash.

blocks.sentence: Money a company has earned but not yet collected from customers sits on the balance sheet as accounts ___.
blocks.explanation: Accounts receivable represents revenue that's already been recognized as earned but hasn't been collected in cash yet.

blocks.robotComment: Growing sales on credit feels like success — and it can turn into a cash problem if it grows faster than collections. ⏳
blocks.body: This is exactly why the cash flow statement adjusts net income for the change in accounts receivable — a growing receivables balance means more of reported profit is still sitting with customers rather than in the bank. A company can be profitable and still run into a real cash crunch if too much of its profit is tied up this way, which is one reason lenders and investors watch the cash flow statement so closely, not just net income.

highlights.text: profitable and still run into a real cash crunch

blocks.question: A company makes a $10 million sale on credit, with the customer paying in 90 days. What happens immediately, under standard accounting rules?
options: Revenue and profit are recognized now, but no cash has been received yet
Nothing happens until the cash is actually received
The sale is recorded as a liability
The company must wait 90 days to report any revenue
blocks.explanation: Accounting recognizes revenue when it's earned, not when cash is collected — the $10M shows up as profit now and as accounts receivable until it's paid.

blocks.statement: A company can report strong net income for a period and still have very little actual cash on hand.
blocks.explanation: This is exactly the gap this lesson covers — profit recognized on paper doesn't guarantee the cash has actually been collected yet.

lessons.title: Reading a Real Statement: A Guided Walkthrough

blocks.robotComment: Once you've read one of these carefully, the next one is far less intimidating. 📄
blocks.body: Real filings use more granular line-item names than the simplified versions used so far in this level, but the underlying logic is identical. This lesson walks through Brightleaf's income statement the way it might actually appear in a real filing, line by line.

Start at the top and work down. "Revenue" is total sales for the year. "Cost of Revenue" (or cost of goods sold) is what it directly cost to deliver those sales. Subtracting the two gives "Gross Profit." From there, "Operating Expenses" — salaries, marketing, rent — get subtracted to reach "Operating Income," also sometimes labeled EBIT. Finally, "Interest Expense" and the "Provision for Income Taxes" are subtracted to land on "Net Income," the last line.

code.code:
Revenue                              $500M
Cost of Revenue                      -$200M
------------------------------------------
Gross Profit                          $300M

Operating Expenses                    -$180M
------------------------------------------
Operating Income (EBIT)                $120M

Interest Expense                       -$20M
------------------------------------------
Income Before Taxes                    $100M

Provision for Income Taxes              -$25M
------------------------------------------
Net Income                              $75M
code.caption: Brightleaf's income statement with filing-style line items — the same $75M net income as before, now with interest and taxes shown separately instead of combined.

blocks.sentence: On a real filing, the line often labeled "Provision for Income ___" represents the taxes a company owes on its pre-tax income.
blocks.explanation: The "Provision for Income Taxes" line represents the estimated tax expense for the period, subtracted to arrive at net income.

blocks.body: A useful habit when reading any real statement for the first time: don't try to absorb every number at once. Find revenue first, find net income last, and then work out what happened between those two lines — that's usually where the real story about a company's costs, efficiency, and profitability lives.

highlights.text: Find revenue first, find net income last

blocks.question: On Brightleaf's filing-style income statement, what is "Income Before Taxes"?
blocks.explanation: Operating Income of $120M minus $20M in interest expense equals $100M in income before taxes.

blocks.statement: Real company filings use fundamentally different logic from the simplified income statement examples used earlier in this level.
blocks.explanation: The line-item names get more specific, but the underlying logic — revenue down to net income, step by step — is exactly the same.
